title: Kings, Seek Wisdom
sum: The speaker turns back to the rulers of the earth he addressed in 1:1. Their power was lent to them by the Lord, who will examine how they used it; the more power they had, the stricter their test will be, for God made small and great alike. So they should learn wisdom.

Then Wisdom herself comes into view: she shines and never fades, she is easily found, she even goes looking for those worthy of her and waits at their gates. A chain of steps leads from longing for instruction to love, to keeping her laws, to incorruption, to nearness to God, to a kingdom. The chapter ends with a promise: the speaker will tell, openly and without envy, what Wisdom is and how she came to be.
readings: Read as advice to rulers

The chapter belongs to a well-known kind of Greek writing, the address to kings on how to rule. It tells them their power is God's gift and that God will hold them to account. Read this way it agrees with Romans 13:1 and with the prophets' words to kings.
Read as an invitation to everyone

The 'kings' may be a literary frame. The real readers were ordinary Jews in a Greek city, and the promise of 6:20–21, a kingdom through wisdom, is the reign of the righteous with God that the book has promised (3:8; 5:16). On this reading every reader is a king in training.

views.C: The Catholic Church reads 6:12–16 at Mass on the 32nd Sunday in Ordinary Time (Year A), beside the parable of the ten bridesmaids, and 6:1–11 on a weekday of the 32nd week. Wisdom going out to meet those who seek her is read as a picture of God's grace that comes first.
views.O: The Orthodox churches count Wisdom among the books read in church (the 'readable' books), though not with the full authority of the Hebrew canon in every Orthodox teacher. They read Wisdom here, as elsewhere, of Christ, the Wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24).
views.P: Protestants do not count the book as Scripture, but its teaching on rulers matches Proverbs 8:15–16 and Romans 13:1–4, and many read it as sound wisdom. The chain of 6:17–20 is often compared with Romans 5:3–5.
views.H: Scholars see in the chapter the Greek form of advice to kings and the philosophers' chain argument (sorites). The phrase 'incorruption puts a person close to God' (6:19) draws on Greek ideas of becoming like God, set inside Jewish faith in the God who judges.
views.J: Jewish readers have not used the book in the synagogue, since it is not in the Hebrew Bible, but its teaching that rulers answer to God is shared with the Psalms (Psalm 2:10; 82) and later Jewish teaching on kings.

echoes: Psalm 2:10; Proverbs 8:1–21; Romans 13:1–4; Daniel 2:21; John 19:11; Proverbs 1:20–33; Romans 5:3–5; 1 Corinthians 15:53

settings.by: The book's speaker, whom 7:1–9:18 shows to be Solomon
settings.to: Kings and judges of the earth, as the book addresses them
settings.when: after the judgment scene of chapters 2–5
settings.why: To warn rulers that their power is on loan from God, and to win them to wisdom, which leads to a lasting kingdom. Knowing that the real readers were not kings, the warning becomes comfort: the powerful who oppress the righteous will answer to God, and the humble who love Wisdom will reign.
settings.readers: Greek-speaking Jews, most likely in Alexandria in Egypt, a city of Greek schools, mystery cults and rulers who claimed divine favor. Most scholars place the book in the last centuries BC or the early first century AD (the book's front page gives the dates proposed). For such readers the speech showed that the wisdom of Israel's God was the best of all wisdom, worthy of kings and philosophers.
views: Some think the book was meant, at least in part, for Gentile rulers or educated Greeks, to commend Jewish wisdom to them.
Most scholars think the address to kings is a convention, and the book was written for Jews, to strengthen them in their faith in a Greek city.

title: A Breath of the Power of God
sum: Now the speaker talks about himself. He is a mortal like everyone, born the same way and bound for the same death. So he prayed, and a spirit of wisdom came to him. He chose her over thrones and gold, and with her came every good thing. She taught him all the sciences of his day: the structure of the world, the elements, the calendar, the stars, animals, plants and the human mind.

The chapter then describes Wisdom herself, with twenty-one marks of her spirit, and with images that became central to Christian thought about the Son: she is a vapor of God's power, an outflow of his glory, a radiance of eternal light, a stainless mirror of his working and an image of his goodness. She is one, yet she can do all things and makes all things new; in every age she passes into holy souls and makes them friends of God and prophets.
readings: Read as Jewish wisdom in Greek dress

The king of 1 Kings 3 prays and receives wisdom, but the wisdom he receives is described in the language of Greek philosophy: a fine spirit that runs through all things, as the Stoics said, and an outflow of divine light. The writer claims that everything good in Greek learning comes from Israel's God.
Read with the New Testament

Christians have read 7:22–8:1 beside Hebrews 1:3, Colossians 1:15–17 and John 1:1–9. What Wisdom is here, the Son is there: the radiance of God's glory, his image, the one through whom all things were made. Most scholars think the New Testament writers drew on this Jewish picture of Wisdom to speak of Christ.

views.C: The Catholic Lectionary reads 7:7–11 on the 28th Sunday in Ordinary Time (Year B) and 7:22b–8:1 on a weekday of the 32nd week, and 7:7–10, 15–16 on the feasts of doctors of the Church such as Thomas Aquinas. The images of 7:25–26 are applied to the Son in the Church's tradition.
views.O: The Orthodox read Wisdom's titles in this chapter of Christ, the Wisdom of God, to whom the great church of Constantinople, Hagia Sophia, was dedicated. Origen, read in the East, explained 7:25–26 of the Son.
views.P: Protestants read the chapter as a witness to Jewish thought that shaped the New Testament's language about Christ (Hebrews 1:3; Colossians 1:15), while basing doctrine on the New Testament texts themselves.
views.H: Scholars study the chapter as a meeting of Jewish wisdom and Greek philosophy, especially Stoic ideas of a divine spirit pervading the world and Platonic ideas of light and image. Many see it as the most important source for the 'wisdom christology' of the New Testament.
views.J: Jewish thinkers of the same city, above all Philo of Alexandria, spoke of God's Wisdom and Word in similar ways. Later rabbinic Judaism identified divine wisdom with the Torah rather than with a heavenly figure.

deep.b: Counting the Greek, the spirit in Wisdom has twenty adjectives and one participle phrase: twenty-one, three times seven. Some describe her mind (intelligent, clear, distinct, sharp), some her purity (holy, unstained, beyond harm, pure), some her power (unstoppable, all-powerful, watching over all), some her goodness (loving the good, doing good, kind to people), and some her movement (quick-moving, fine, making her way through every spirit). The list moves from what she is to what she does, and 7:24–8:1 then explains: she pervades all things because she is pure, and she can do this because she comes from God himself.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the mirror and the image as a teaching order
deep.b: This is my own suggestion, not a view I have found stated in this form. The five images of 7:25–26 seem to move from the most material to the most personal: a vapor (something rising from a source), an outflow (something streaming from it), a radiance (light shining from light), a mirror (something that shows another), and an image (something that is like another). Read in that order, the passage teaches a reader step by step that Wisdom is from God, then like God, then the way God is seen. Hebrews 1:3 and Colossians 1:15 take only the last steps, radiance and image, which may be why they chose them. Many scholars note the images; the ordering is my reading.

echoes: 1 Kings 3:5–14; 1 Kings 4:29–34; Proverbs 8:22–31; Hebrews 1:3; Colossians 1:15–17; John 1:1–14; 1 Corinthians 1:24; James 1:5; James 1:17; Revelation 21:5

settings.what: Solomon's speech about how he found Wisdom
settings.by: Solomon, speaking in the first person, though the book never names him
settings.to: The rulers addressed in 6:1–11, and every reader
settings.when: as the king looks back on his life, from his birth to his prayer at Gibeon
settings.why: To show that even a king is an ordinary mortal, and that his greatness came only from Wisdom, God's gift in answer to prayer. The speech teaches the reader what Wisdom is and how to seek her, and it prepares for the prayer of chapter 9.
settings.readers: Greek-speaking Jews, most likely in Alexandria in Egypt, a city of Greek schools, mystery cults and rulers who claimed divine favor. Most scholars place the book in the last centuries BC or the early first century AD (the book's front page gives the dates proposed). For such readers the speech showed that the wisdom of Israel's God was the best of all wisdom, worthy of kings and philosophers.

title: Wisdom as a Bride
sum: Solomon tells how he fell in love with Wisdom when he was young and wanted to bring her home as his bride. She lives with God and knows his secrets; she is richer than wealth, the craftswoman of all things, the teacher of the four great virtues, wise in history, speech and the future. With her he would be honored by elders, feared by rulers, and remembered forever; with her at home there would be no bitterness, only joy.

He thought it over: there is immortality in being joined to her. He had been a gifted child with a good soul, or better, being good he came into an undefiled body. But he knew he could not win her unless God gave her, and knowing that was itself wisdom. So he turned to the Lord in prayer.
readings: Read as a love story

The language is that of courtship and marriage: he loves her, seeks her as a bride, brings her home, rests with her. Solomon, known for his many wives (1 Kings 11:1–4), is pictured as the man whose one true bride was Wisdom.
Read as a philosophy of the soul

Verses 19–20 speak of a good soul and a body it entered, language that sounds like Plato. Whether the writer believed that souls exist before bodies is one of the book's most debated questions (see the card).

views.C: Catholic teaching reads 8:19–20 without a pre-existence of souls: each soul is created immediately by God (Catechism 366). The Latin 'I could not be continent unless God gave it' (8:21) shaped Augustine's teaching on grace and the Western tradition after him.
views.O: Orthodox teaching holds that soul and body come into being together (John of Damascus) and rejects Origen's teaching that souls existed first. The chapter's bridal language is read of the soul's love for God's Wisdom, Christ.
views.P: Protestants read 8:21 as true teaching that wisdom is God's gift (James 1:5), and most see in 8:19–20 a Greek idea of the soul that goes beyond the Bible. Reformed and Lutheran theologians long debated where souls come from (see the card).
views.H: Scholars note the Greek education behind the chapter: the four cardinal virtues (8:7), the rhetoric of praise, and a view of the soul close to Plato's. Many think 8:19–20 does imply the soul's existence before the body; others think the writer is not stating a theory.
views.J: The Talmud reports Rav Asi's teaching that the Messiah, son of David, "will not come until all the souls of the body have been finished," that is, until every soul destined for a body has entered one (Bavli Yevamot 62a). That implies souls waiting before birth, a view close to one reading of 8:19–20, which is centuries older.

echoes: Proverbs 4:6–9; Proverbs 7:4; Proverbs 8:30; Proverbs 31:10–31; 1 Kings 3:7; 1 Kings 10:1; 1 Kings 11:1–4; Song of Songs 4:9; James 1:5

traditions.q: Solomon says, "a good soul was given me as my share. Or better, since I was good, I came into a body without stain" (8:19–20). Does the soul exist before the body, and where does each soul come from? (Whether the soul is immortal by nature or by God's gift is asked on the card at chapter 3.)
views: No soul exists before its body. "Every spiritual soul is created immediately by God" and is not produced by the parents (Catechism 366). The anathemas against Origen that come down with the Second Council of Constantinople (553) begin by condemning "the fabulous pre-existence of souls."

Soul and body come into being together: John of Damascus teaches that "body and soul were formed at one and the same time, not first the one and then the other," as Origen supposed (Exact Exposition 2.12). Origen's pre-existence of souls was condemned in the anathemas of 553.

Divided over where souls come from, agreed against pre-existence. Charles Hodge reports that the Formula of Concord favors creation of each soul by God, but that most Lutheran theologians of the 1600s taught traducianism, that the soul is passed on from the parents with the body.

Each soul is created by God and joined to the body. Hodge calls this the common doctrine of the church and especially of the Reformed, held by Calvin, Beza, Turretin and most Reformed theologians, and he rejects pre-existence as a teaching that "began and ended with Origen" and has no basis in Scripture.

Yes: human spirits lived with God before their birth on earth. "Man was also in the beginning with God. Intelligence, or the light of truth, was not created or made, neither indeed can be" (Doctrine and Covenants 93:29).

deep.h: Origen and the soul before the body
deep.b: Origen of Alexandria (about AD 185–254) taught that God first made all rational beings equal and alike, and that their different states in this world come from the free choices they made before it: "God, who deemed it just to arrange His creatures according to their merit, brought down these different understandings into the harmony of one world" (On First Principles 2.9.6). He supported this from Jacob and Esau, chosen "before they were born" (Romans 9:11; On First Principles 2.9.7). The church rejected the idea: the anathemas against Origen of the 500s begin with it, and John of Damascus wrote against it. Augustine, Hodge notes, was drawn toward traducianism in his debate with Pelagius but "never, however, could bring himself fully to adopt it."

settings.when: as he recalls his youth before his prayer
settings.why: To make the reader want Wisdom as a lover wants a bride, and to show that even the best natural gifts are not enough: Wisdom must be asked from God. The closing verse (8:21) turns the whole speech into a lesson on prayer.

title: Give Me Wisdom
sum: This is Solomon's prayer for wisdom, the prayer at Gibeon of 1 Kings 3 and 2 Chronicles 1, now told at length. God made all things by his word and formed human beings by his wisdom to rule the world justly. 'Give me Wisdom, who sits beside you on your thrones.' The king is God's slave, weak and short-lived; even a perfect man counts for nothing without God's wisdom. God chose him as king and told him to build a temple, a copy of the holy tent prepared from the beginning. Wisdom was with God at creation: 'Send her' to labor with me.

The last part widens to all humanity. No one can know God's plan; our reasonings are timid, the perishable body weighs the soul down, we hardly understand the earth, let alone heaven. Only if God gives wisdom and sends his Holy Spirit can anyone know his will. That is how those on earth were set on straight paths and saved by wisdom.
readings: Read as Solomon's prayer

The prayer follows 1 Kings 3:6–9 closely: God's mercy, the king's weakness and youth, the great people he must judge, the request for wisdom. But it adds what Kings does not have: Wisdom as a person beside God's throne, the heavenly tent, and a meditation on human limits.
Read as everyone's prayer

From 9:13 the 'I' becomes 'we': the prayer belongs to every human being. The Catholic Church reads 9:13–18 on a Sunday and in the rite of anointing of the sick, as the prayer of anyone who must decide without seeing the way.

views.C: The Catholic Lectionary reads 9:13–18b on the 23rd Sunday in Ordinary Time (Year C), and 9:9–11, 13–18 at the anointing of the sick. Augustine quoted 9:15 often, and the verse shaped Western teaching that the body as it now is, after sin, burdens the soul.
views.O: Orthodox readers take the prayer as a model for all who seek God's wisdom, and 9:17's pairing of wisdom and the Holy Spirit as a witness to the Spirit who gives wisdom.
views.P: Protestants hear in 9:13–17 the same teaching as 1 Corinthians 2:10–16: God's mind is known only by his Spirit. Many see in 9:15 a Greek view of the body that Paul's hope of resurrection corrects (2 Corinthians 5:1–4).
views.H: Scholars note how the writer retells 1 Kings 3 in the light of Greek philosophy: the body as the soul's burden (Plato, Phaedo 81c), and the heavenly model of the temple, a theme also found in Hebrews 8:5.
views.J: Jewish readers recognize the prayer of 1 Kings 3 and the teaching of a heavenly sanctuary that the earthly temple copies (Exodus 25:9, 40), an idea developed in later Jewish writings.

echoes: 1 Kings 3:5–14; 2 Chronicles 1:7–12; Exodus 25:9; Exodus 25:40; Hebrews 8:5; Isaiah 40:13; Romans 11:33–34; 1 Corinthians 2:10–16; 2 Corinthians 5:1–4; Psalm 116:16

settings.to: God, "God of my fathers, Lord of your mercy"
settings.when: at the start of his reign, before he built the temple (as at Gibeon, 1 Kings 3:5)
settings.why: To ask for Wisdom as God's gift, and to teach readers to ask the same. Knowing that the hearers were Jews in a Greek city, the prayer says that the highest knowledge, of God's will, is not reached by philosophy alone but given from above.
settings.readers: Greek-speaking Jews, most likely in Alexandria in Egypt, a city of Greek schools, mystery cults and rulers who claimed divine favor. title: Wisdom Saves the Righteous
sum: Without naming anyone, the chapter retells history from Adam to the Exodus as the story of Wisdom. She guarded the first-formed man and rescued him from his trespass. Cain left her and perished; because of him the earth was flooded, and she steered Noah on a bit of wood. When the nations were confused at Babel, she found Abraham and made him strong at the binding of Isaac. She rescued Lot from the fire on the Five Cities, whose smoking land and pillar of salt still stand as witnesses.

She led Jacob, fleeing his brother, showed him God's kingdom, made him rich and gave him the prize in his wrestling. She went down with Joseph into the pit and brought him a kingdom's scepters. She entered the soul of Moses, faced Pharaoh with signs, paid the slaves their wages, was their cloud and fire, brought them through the Red Sea and drowned their enemies. The righteous sang, and Wisdom opened the mouths of the mute and of babies.
readings: Read as retold history

Each hero is 'a righteous man' saved by Wisdom, each villain one who left her. The chapter adds details Genesis does not have (Adam rescued, Cain perished, the Flood because of him, the infants' song) that come from Jewish retellings of the stories.
Read as a pattern

With no names given, the stories become types: the righteous suffer, are guarded and are raised; the wicked destroy themselves. The pattern prepares for chapters 11–19, where Egypt and Israel are set side by side in seven contrasts.

views.C: Catholic readers see Wisdom's work in the patriarchs as God's saving plan running through history toward Christ, and the chapter as a model of reading the Old Testament through its types.
views.O: Orthodox readers, who honor the forefathers in the liturgy, read the chapter as Christ, God's Wisdom, at work in the righteous before his coming; icons of the resurrection show Christ raising Adam, whom 10:1 says Wisdom rescued.
views.P: Protestants compare the chapter with Hebrews 11, where faith, not Wisdom, is the thread through the same heroes, and note where the chapter goes beyond Genesis.
views.H: Scholars read the chapter as an early example of Jewish 'rewritten Bible' and of the example list, a form known from Greek rhetoric and from Sirach 44–50 and Hebrews 11. Some suggest the heroes are left unnamed so that the pattern, not the name, carries the lesson.
views.J: Several details match later Jewish tradition: the Egyptians' weapons washed ashore for Israel (Josephus, Antiquities 2.349) and the infants who sang at the sea (Bavli Sotah 30b). Wisdom is an early witness to these traditions.

echoes: Genesis 2–4; Genesis 6–9; Genesis 11–12; Genesis 19; Genesis 22; Genesis 27–33; Genesis 37–41; Exodus 3–15; Hebrews 11:1–31; Sirach 44–50; Acts 7:2–36

settings.what: Wisdom in history, from Adam to the Exodus
settings.by: The book's speaker, turning in 10:20 to address the Lord
settings.to: The readers, and at 10:20 God himself
settings.when: after the prayer for wisdom (9:18 'saved by wisdom')
settings.why: To prove the prayer's last line: Wisdom has always saved those who served her and ruined those who left her. For Jews living in Egypt, the climax, Israel rescued from Egypt, was their own founding story set in their own land.
